**Non-inferiority only:**

- **ROCKET AF** (rivaroxaban): non-inferiority in the per-protocol as-treated primary analysis (188 vs 241 events; 1.7%/yr vs 2.2%/yr; HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66–0.96, P<0.001 for non-inferiority); in the intention-to-treat analysis HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.74–1.03) with P=0.12 for superiority. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"In patients with atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban was noninferior to warfarin for the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism."} -->

**Meta-analysis (four pivotal DOAC trials — RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48; 71,683 participants):** compared with warfarin, new oral anticoagulants reduced haemorrhagic stroke (RR 0·49, 95% CI 0·38–0·64; p<0·0001), all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85–0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39–0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01–1·55; p=0·04). The overall 19% reduction in stroke or systemic embolism (0·81, 0·73–0·91) was mainly driven by the haemorrhagic stroke reduction. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001)"} -->

**Consistency with the individual trials:** yes, in direction and approximate size.
- RE-LY: haemorrhagic stroke 0·38%/yr with warfarin vs 0·12%/yr (dabigatran 110 mg) and 0·10%/yr (150 mg), both P<0·001; mortality 4·13% vs 3.75% (P=0·13) and 3.64% (P=0·051). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.38% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 0.12% per year with 110 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001) and 0.10% per year with 150 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001)."} -->
- ARISTOTLE: haemorrhagic stroke 0·24%/yr vs 0·47%/yr (HR 0·51, 0·35–0·75; P<0·001) and lower all-cause mortality (HR 0·89, 0·80–0·99; P=0·047). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.24% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 0.47% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.75; P<0.001)"} -->

Both trials' point estimates for haemorrhagic stroke (roughly 0·5 in ARISTOTLE) sit within the pooled 0·49 (0·38–0·64), so the meta-analysis is consistent with them. Note that RE-LY's mortality reduction was not individually significant, whereas the pooled mortality effect was.

**Low-dose edoxaban in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48** (Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation): the annualized rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban vs 1.50% with warfarin (HR 1.07; 97.5% CI 0.87–1.31; P=0.005 for noninferiority), i.e. noninferior to warfarin for efficacy. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 1.07; 97.5% confidence interval [CI], 0.87 to 1.31; P=0.005 for noninferiority)"} --> In the intention-to-treat analysis there was an unfavourable trend versus warfarin (HR 1.13; 97.5% CI 0.96–1.34; P=0.10). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"an unfavorable trend with low-dose edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio, 1.13; 97.5% CI, 0.96 to 1.34; P=0.10)"} --> Major bleeding was 1.61% vs 3.43% with warfarin (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.41–0.55; P<0.001). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)"} -->

**Pooled low-dose regimens in the four-trial meta-analysis** (Comparison of the efficacy and safety of new oral anticoagulants with warfarin…): low-dose NOAC regimens showed similar overall reductions in stroke or systemic embolic events to warfarin (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.84–1.27; p=0.74) and a more favourable bleeding profile (0.65, 0.43–1.00; p=0.05), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (1.28, 1.02–1.60; p=0.045). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"Low-dose new oral anticoagulant regimens showed similar overall reductions in stroke or systemic embolic events to warfarin (1·03, 0·84-1·27; p=0·74), and a more favourable bleeding profile (0·65, 0·43-1·00; p=0·05), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (1·28, 1·02-1·60; p=0·045)."} -->

- **14,264 patients** with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation at increased risk of stroke were randomly assigned, in a double-blind trial, to rivaroxaban or dose-adjusted warfarin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"we randomly assigned 14,264 patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation who were at increased risk for stroke"} -->

In ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, 21,105 patients with moderate-to-high-risk atrial fibrillation were randomized (median follow-up 2.8 years) to one of two once-daily edoxaban regimens or warfarin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"comparing two once-daily regimens of edoxaban with warfarin in 21,105 patients with moderate-to-high-risk atrial fibrillation (median follow-up, 2.8 years)"} -->

In the warfarin group, the median time in the therapeutic range was 68.4% (during treatment, with an annualized primary-endpoint rate of 1.50%). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of the primary end point during treatment was 1.50% with warfarin (median time in the therapeutic range, 68.4%)"} -->

answer:
**Short answer: in the individual trials, cardiovascular death on its own was not clearly reduced — the benefit was driven mainly by hospitalization for heart failure. Only when the trials are pooled does CV death reach significance.**

**DELIVER** (dapagliflozin, LVEF >40%, 6263 patients): primary composite HR 0.82 (0.73–0.92), but cardiovascular death alone occurred in 231 (7.4%) vs 261 (8.3%), HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.74–1.05) — not significant.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"cardiovascular death occurred in 231 patients (7.4%) and 261 patients (8.3%), respectively (hazard ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.05)"} -->

**EMPEROR-Preserved** (empagliflozin, preserved EF): primary outcome HR 0.79 (0.69–0.90), and the paper states the effect "was mainly related to a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure" — i.e., CV death was not the driver.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"This effect was mainly related to a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure in the empagliflozin group."} -->

**DAPA-HF** (dapagliflozin, LVEF ≤40%): the knowledge base reports only the composite primary outcome (worsening HF or CV death) and its conclusion that this risk was lower; it gives no separate hazard ratio for CV death alone, so I can't quantify that component for DAPA-HF.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo"} -->

**Meta-analysis** (five trials, 21,947 participants): CV death was reduced on its own — HR 0.87 (0.79–0.95) — alongside the composite 0.77 (0.72–0.82), first HF hospitalization 0.72 (0.67–0.78) and all-cause mortality 0.92 (0.86–0.99).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])"} -->

In the HFmrEF/HFpEF subset alone (DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved, 12,251 participants), the CV death reduction was borderline — HR 0.88 (0.77–1.00), the confidence interval touching 1 — versus first HF hospitalization 0.74 (0.67–0.83).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])"} -->

So: at the individual-trial level, mortality benefit was not demonstrated (and in EMPEROR-Preserved the effect was attributed mainly to HF hospitalization); the pooled analysis, especially across all five trials, did show a modest significant reduction in CV death.

Renal-specific composite (ESKD, doubling of creatinine, or renal death) reduced by 34% (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.53–0.81).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"The relative risk of the renal-specific composite of end-stage kidney disease, a doubling of the creatinine level, or death from renal causes was lower by 34% (hazard ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.81; P<0.001)"} -->

**DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin):** 4304 participants with eGFR 25–75 and albumin-to-creatinine ratio 200–5000; included patients with and without type 2 diabetes.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"We randomly assigned 4304 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 25 to 75 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of 200 to 5000"} -->
Effects were similar with and without type 2 diabetes.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->

**EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin):** the broadest entry — eGFR ≥20 to <45, or eGFR ≥45 to <90 with albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥200, so it enrolled patients with lower eGFR and, in the lower-eGFR stratum, without requiring albuminuria.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio"} -->
Results were consistent with or without diabetes and across eGFR ranges.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->

In short: CREDENCE was diabetes-only with heavy albuminuria and mid-range eGFR; DAPA-CKD required substantial albuminuria (ACR ≥200) over eGFR 25–75 and included non-diabetic patients; EMPA-KIDNEY extended to eGFR as low as 20 and to non-albuminuric patients at higher eGFR. answer:
**Reduction in all-cause death**

- The five-trial meta-analysis (21,947 participants) found SGLT2 inhibitors reduced all-cause mortality: HR 0·92 (95% CI 0·86–0·99), alongside cardiovascular death 0·87 (0·79–0·95) and CV death or HF hospitalisation 0·77 (0·72–0·82). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0-99])"} -->

**No significant difference in all-cause death**

- Empagliflozin in chronic kidney disease: no significant between-group difference in death from any cause (4.5% vs 5.1%), nor in the composite of HF hospitalisation or CV death (4.0% vs 4.6%); hospitalisation from any cause was lower (HR 0.86; 0.78–0.95). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"there were no significant between-group differences with respect to the composite outcome of hospitalization for heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes (which occurred in 4.0% in the empagliflozin group and 4.6% in the placebo group) or death from any cause (in 4.5% and 5.1%, respectively)"} -->

- **DELIVER** (EF >40%): 16.4% vs 19.5%, HR 0.82 (0.73–0.92), P<0.001, median 2.3 years; worsening HF HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91), CV death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the EF range:** the benefit is consistent but somewhat attenuated at higher EF (0.74 and 0.75 in reduced EF vs 0.79 and 0.82 in preserved). In the five-trial meta-analysis (21,947 participants), the composite was reduced with HR 0.77 (0.72–0.82), and "Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} --> In DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved combined (12,251 participants), the composite HR was 0.80 (0.73–0.87), with CV death 0.88 (0.77–1.00) and first HF hospitalization 0.74 (0.67–0.83). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87])"} -->

Note: the individual-trial CV-death components were not uniformly significant (DELIVER 0.88, 0.74–1.05; pooled preserved-EF 0.88, 0.77–1.00), so the preserved-EF benefit rests largely on HF hospitalization.

**No significant difference in all-cause death:**

- **EMPA-KIDNEY** (empagliflozin, CKD): no significant between-group difference for death from any cause (4.5% vs 5.1%). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"but there were no significant between-group differences with respect to the composite outcome of hospitalization for heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes (which occurred in 4.0% in the empagliflozin group and 4.6% in the placebo group) or death from any cause (in 4.5% and 5.1%, respectively)"} -->

- EMPA-KIDNEY: HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.64–0.82) for kidney progression or CV death, consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across eGFR subgroups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->

The knowledge base gives no head-to-head comparison of the three trials and no separate diabetes-versus-non-diabetes hazard ratios beyond the statements quoted.

In DAPA-CKD, the number needed to treat to prevent one primary outcome event was **19 (95% CI, 15 to 27)**, over a median follow-up of 2.4 years.

This applies to the composite primary outcome (sustained decline in eGFR of ≥50%, end-stage kidney disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes), which occurred in 197 of 2152 dapagliflozin participants (9.2%) versus 312 of 2152 placebo participants (14.5%); hazard ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.51–0.72), P<0.001.

answer:
**Reduction in all-cause death:** only the heart-failure meta-analysis of five SGLT2-inhibitor trials reports it — in 21,947 participants, all-cause mortality was reduced (HR 0·92, 95% CI 0·86–0·99), alongside cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79–0·95]). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])"} --> Within the narrower DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved set (12,251 participants) the effect on cardiovascular death was of borderline significance (0·88 [0·77–1·00]). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00])"} -->

**No significant difference / not reported for all-cause death:** the individual SGLT2 trials in the knowledge base (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced, EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER, DAPA-CKD, CREDENCE) report only composite endpoints built on cardiovascular, renal or heart-failure events, not all-cause mortality; the meta-analysis is the only source here giving an all-cause mortality result. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"death from renal or cardiovascular causes was significantly lower with dapagliflozin than with placebo"} -->

**Short answer: not consistently. The benefit on cardiovascular death alone was clear only in reduced ejection fraction (DAPA-HF) and only became statistically significant when the five trials were pooled; in the preserved/mildly reduced EF trials it was not significant (DELIVER) or was not the driver of benefit (EMPEROR-Preserved).**

- **DAPA-HF (EF ≤40%):** death from cardiovascular causes 227 (9.6%) vs 273 (11.5%), HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.69–0.98) — a significant reduction, alongside a first worsening HF event HR of 0.70 (0.59–0.83). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98)"} -->
- **DELIVER (EF >40%):** cardiovascular death 231 (7.4%) vs 261 (8.3%), HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05) — not significant; the significant component was worsening HF, HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91), with the composite primary outcome HR 0.82 (0.73–0.92). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"cardiovascular death occurred in 231 patients (7.4%) and 261 patients (8.3%), respectively (hazard ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.05)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved (EF >40%):** composite CV death or HF hospitalization HR 0.79 (0.69–0.90), but "this effect was mainly related to a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure"; total HF hospitalizations HR 0.73 (0.61–0.88). No separate CV-death estimate is given. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"This effect was mainly related to a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure in the empagliflozin group."} -->
- **Meta-analysis of five trials (n=21,947):** CV death HR 0.87 (0.79–0.95) and all-cause mortality 0.92 (0.86–0.99), alongside first HF hospitalization 0.72 (0.67–0.78) and the composite 0.77 (0.72–0.82). In the two preserved-EF trials alone (n=12,251), CV death was 0.88 (0.77–1.00) — borderline, consistent in direction but not clearly significant — versus HF hospitalization 0.74 (0.67–0.83). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])"} -->

So: the mortality benefit is smaller and less certain than the hospitalization benefit, is statistically robust only in reduced EF individually and across all five trials pooled, and in preserved EF the reduction is driven mainly by fewer heart failure hospitalizations.

**Heart failure trials**

- **DAPA-HF (dapagliflozin, HFrEF):** adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups."} -->
- **DELIVER (dapagliflozin, HFmrEF/HFpEF):** the incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups."} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin):** uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->
- **EMPEROR-Reduced (empagliflozin):** uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"Uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->

**Chronic kidney disease trials**

- **EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin):** the rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"The rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups."} -->
- **DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin):** the known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed."} -->
- **CREDENCE (canagliflozin, T2D with albuminuric CKD):** there were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"There were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture."} -->

**Where no difference was found:** volume depletion, renal dysfunction and hypoglycemia events (DAPA-HF), overall adverse-event incidence (DELIVER), serious adverse events (EMPA-KIDNEY), and amputation/fracture (CREDENCE).

The documents do not report specific rates of ketoacidosis or other adverse events beyond those listed above.

The only all-cause mortality findings in the knowledge base come from aspirin documents (for example, higher all-cause mortality with aspirin in ASPREE), not from SGLT2 inhibitor studies.

This corresponds to primary outcome events in 197 of 2152 participants (9.2%) on dapagliflozin versus 312 of 2152 (14.5%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.72).

answer:
**Kidney function (eGFR) entry ranges**
- CREDENCE: eGFR 30 to <90 ml/min/1.73 m² — all patients had type 2 diabetes and albuminuria (ACR >300 to 5000 mg/g), on RAS blockade. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"All the patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30 to <90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000)"} -->
- DAPA-CKD: eGFR 25 to 75 ml/min/1.73 m² with ACR 200 to 5000 mg/g; 4304 participants. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"We randomly assigned 4304 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 25 to 75 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of 200 to 5000"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: eGFR ≥20 to <45, or eGFR ≥45 to <90 with ACR ≥200 mg/g — i.e., it included patients with lower eGFR and, via the eGFR-only arm, patients without marked albuminuria. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200"} -->

**Albuminuria:** CREDENCE required the highest albuminuria (ACR >300 mg/g); DAPA-CKD required ACR 200–5000 mg/g; EMPA-KIDNEY required ACR ≥200 mg/g only for those with eGFR 45–<90, so it was the only one of the three open to normoalbuminuric patients with low eGFR.

**Diabetes status:** CREDENCE enrolled only patients with type 2 diabetes. DAPA-CKD and EMPA-KIDNEY enrolled patients with and without diabetes.

**Consistency of effect with and without diabetes**
- DAPA-CKD: effects were similar in participants with and without type 2 diabetes, and benefit was seen regardless of diabetes status. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across eGFR subgroups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->
- CREDENCE cannot speak to the non-diabetic question, since all its participants had type 2 diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"In patients with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease, the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular events was lower in the canagliflozin group than in the placebo group at a median follow-up of 2.62 years."} -->

The knowledge base does not give the specific hazard ratios for the with-diabetes versus without-diabetes subgroups in DAPA-CKD or EMPA-KIDNEY, nor the proportion of diabetic patients in each trial.

answer:
**Heart failure (DAPA-HF, dapagliflozin):** the frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction and hypoglycemia did not differ between dapagliflozin and placebo — that is where no difference was found. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups."} -->

**Chronic kidney disease (EMPA-KIDNEY, empagliflozin):** the rates of serious adverse events were similar in the empagliflozin and placebo groups. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"The rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups."} -->

**Chronic kidney disease (DAPA-CKD, dapagliflozin):** no new safety signal was reported; the trial states only that the known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed."} -->

The knowledge base does not give specific adverse-event rates or named safety signals (e.g., ketoacidosis, amputation, genital infections) for these SGLT2 inhibitor trials, nor any adverse-event findings from the preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure trials or the SGLT2 meta-analysis.

**Kidney function (eGFR entry criteria)**
- CREDENCE (canagliflozin): eGFR 30 to <90 ml/min/1.73 m². <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"All the patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30 to <90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000)"} -->
- DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin): eGFR 25–75 ml/min/1.73 m². <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"We randomly assigned 4304 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 25 to 75 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin): eGFR ≥20 to <45, or eGFR ≥45 to <90 with albuminuria. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2"} -->

**Albuminuria**
- CREDENCE required albuminuria with albumin-to-creatinine ratio >300 to 5000 mg/g (all on RAS blockade). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000) and were treated with renin-angiotensin system blockade"} -->
- DAPA-CKD required ACR 200–5000 mg/g. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of 200 to 5000"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: albuminuria (ACR ≥200 mg/g) required only in the higher-eGFR stratum (45 to <90), so it enrolled a broader population including non-albuminuric patients with low eGFR. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200"} -->

**Diabetes status**
- CREDENCE enrolled only patients with type 2 diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"we assigned patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric chronic kidney disease to receive canagliflozin"} -->
- DAPA-CKD enrolled patients with CKD with or without type 2 diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effect of dapagliflozin in patients with chronic kidney disease, with or without type 2 diabetes, is not known."} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY likewise included patients with and without diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->

**Consistency with and without diabetes**
- DAPA-CKD: HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.51–0.72) overall, with similar effects in participants with and without type 2 diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.64–0.82) overall, consistent with or without diabetes and across eGFR ranges. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->
- CREDENCE: HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.82); by design all participants had type 2 diabetes, so no diabetes-free comparison exists. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"the hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.59 to 0.82"} -->

In EMPA-KIDNEY, the primary composite outcome (progression of kidney disease or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 432 of 3304 patients (13.1%) in the empagliflozin group versus 558 of 3305 patients (16.9%) in the placebo group, with a hazard ratio of 0.72 (95% CI, 0.64 to 0.82; P<0.001) over a median follow-up of 2.0 years. The composite was defined as end-stage kidney disease, a sustained decrease in eGFR to <10 ml per minute per 1.73 m², a sustained decrease in eGFR of ≥40% from baseline, or death from renal causes, or death from cardiovascular causes.

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"progression of kidney disease or death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 432 of 3304 patients (13.1%) in the empagliflozin group and in 558 of 3305 patients (16.9%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.64 to 0.82; P<0.001)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"The primary outcome was a composite of progression of kidney disease (defined as end-stage kidney disease, a sustained decrease in eGFR to <10 ml per minute per 1.73 m2, a sustained decrease in eGFR of ≥40% from baseline, or death from renal causes) or death from cardiovascular causes."} -->

Source: "Empagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease" (NEJM, 2023).

**Kidney function (eGFR entry criteria)**
- CREDENCE (canagliflozin): eGFR 30 to <90 ml/min/1.73 m². <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"All the patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30 to <90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000)"} -->
- DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin): eGFR 25–75 ml/min/1.73 m². <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"We randomly assigned 4304 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 25 to 75 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin): eGFR ≥20 to <45, or eGFR ≥45 to <90 with albuminuria. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2"} -->

**Albuminuria**
- CREDENCE required albuminuria with albumin-to-creatinine ratio >300 to 5000 mg/g (all on RAS blockade). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000) and were treated with renin-angiotensin system blockade"} -->
- DAPA-CKD required ACR 200–5000 mg/g. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of 200 to 5000"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: albuminuria (ACR ≥200 mg/g) required only in the higher-eGFR stratum (45 to <90), so it enrolled a broader population including non-albuminuric patients with low eGFR. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200"} -->

**Diabetes status**
- CREDENCE enrolled only patients with type 2 diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"we assigned patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric chronic kidney disease to receive canagliflozin"} -->

**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet; individual participant data, 6 primary prevention trials, ~95,000 people)**

- Aspirin gave a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, or vascular death): 0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001 — i.e. an absolute reduction of about 0.06 percentage points per year, driven mainly by a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18% vs 0.23% per year). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} -->
- Effects on stroke (0.20% vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4) and vascular mortality (0.19% vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7) were not significant. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19%vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7)."} -->

- Net balance framing: explicitly uncertain — "aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds," with further trials awaited. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds"} -->

answer:
**ARRIVE** — 12,546 patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, enrolled at 501 sites in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 or older and women aged 60 or older with average, "moderate" risk based on specific risk factors, excluding those at high bleeding risk or with diabetes. Median follow-up 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

**ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 or older (≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, given 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo; aspirin produced a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage without a significantly lower CVD risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} --> A companion ASPREE analysis also found higher all-cause mortality with aspirin, attributed mainly to cancer-related death. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death."} -->

**JPPP** — 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes, recruited at 1007 clinics between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years; the 5-year cumulative primary outcome rate was not significantly different (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.77–1.15). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups"} -->

**USPSTF** — for adults aged 40 to 59 with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk, the decision to start low-dose aspirin should be individual, since the net benefit is small (C recommendation), and those not at increased bleeding risk who are willing to take it daily are more likely to benefit. For adults 60 or older, the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that there is no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} -->

**Relation to the trials** — the age-60 cutoff maps directly onto the trial populations: ASPREE (≥70, or ≥65 for black and Hispanic participants) and JPPP (60–85) enrolled people at or above 60 and found no cardiovascular benefit, with ASPREE showing more major bleeding (and, in the mortality analysis, higher all-cause mortality), which is the evidence base for the D recommendation. ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60) spans the 40–59 and ≥60 groups, and its null efficacy result with low event rates illustrates the "small net benefit" that makes the 40–59 recommendation an individual decision rather than a routine one. Note that the USPSTF statement concerns adults without CVD or increased bleeding risk, matching the primary-prevention populations of all three trials. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD"} -->

answer:
**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet, individual participant data; 6 primary prevention trials, ~95,000 people)**
- Benefit: 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions (0.18% vs 0.23% per year); net effect on stroke not significant, vascular mortality unchanged (0.19% vs 0.19%). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} -->
- Harm: increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds, 0.10% vs 0.07% per year (p<0.0001). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)"} -->
- Framing: uncertain net value in primary prevention — the reduction in occlusive events must be weighed against the increase in major bleeds. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds."} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials, 164,225 participants, median baseline cardiovascular risk 9.2%)**
- Benefit: composite cardiovascular outcome 57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89 (95% credible interval 0.84–0.95); absolute risk reduction 0.38%; number needed to treat 265. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"(hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)"} -->
- Harm: major bleeding 23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 1.43 (95% credible interval 1.30–1.56); absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"(HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)"} -->
- Framing: not a verdict but a trade-off to discuss — lower cardiovascular risk alongside increased major bleeding, information that "may inform discussions with patients." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

**Comparison:** the two report similar proportional benefit on their (differently defined) vascular composites — 12% relative reduction in 2009 versus HR 0.89 in 2019 — but the bleeding harm is framed more starkly in 2019: a 43% relative increase in major bleeding with an absolute increase (0.47%) slightly larger than the absolute cardiovascular reduction (0.38%), and a number needed to harm (210) smaller than the number needed to treat (265). The 2009 paper expressed the balance qualitatively as "uncertain net value"; the 2019 paper presented both absolute estimates side by side and left the decision to individual patient discussion. Note that the 2009 absolute bleeding figures (0.10% vs 0.07% per year) come from a lower-risk trial population and a different bleeding definition, so they are not directly comparable with the 2019 absolute risks.

answer:
**ARRIVE** — 12,546 patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, enrolled at 501 sites in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 or older and women aged 60 or older with average, "moderate" risk based on specific risk factors, excluding those at high bleeding risk or with diabetes. Median follow-up 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

**ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 or older (≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, given 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo; aspirin produced a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage without a significantly lower CVD risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} --> A companion ASPREE analysis also found higher all-cause mortality with aspirin, attributed mainly to cancer-related death. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death."} -->

**JPPP** — 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes, recruited at 1007 clinics between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years; the 5-year cumulative primary outcome rate was not significantly different (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.77–1.15). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups"} -->

**USPSTF** — for adults aged 40 to 59 with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk, the decision to start low-dose aspirin should be individual, since the net benefit is small (C recommendation), and those not at increased bleeding risk who are willing to take it daily are more likely to benefit. For adults 60 or older, the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that there is no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} -->

**Relation to the trials** — the age-60 cutoff maps directly onto the trial populations: ASPREE (≥70, or ≥65 for black and Hispanic participants) and JPPP (60–85) enrolled people at or above 60 and found no cardiovascular benefit, with ASPREE showing more major bleeding (and, in the mortality analysis, higher all-cause mortality), which is the evidence base for the D recommendation. ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60) spans the 40–59 and ≥60 groups, and its null efficacy result with low event rates illustrates the "small net benefit" that makes the 40–59 recommendation an individual decision rather than a routine one. Note that the USPSTF statement concerns adults without CVD or increased bleeding risk, matching the primary-prevention populations of all three trials. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD"} -->

- 2009: **major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds increased** (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), i.e. an absolute increase of about 0.03% per year; the same coronary risk factors also predicted bleeding. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)" -->

**Comparison and framing of net balance**

- The 2019 analysis puts the absolute bleeding increase (0.47%) slightly above the absolute cardiovascular reduction (0.38%), with NNH 210 vs NNT 265; the 2009 analysis reports a much smaller absolute bleeding excess (~0.03%/year) against a 0.06%/year absolute reduction in serious vascular events, so the two are not directly comparable in absolute terms (different bleeding definitions and outcome composites).

- 2019 framing: aspirin was **associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding**, and this information "may inform discussions with patients" — i.e., a shared decision-making framing rather than a verdict of uncertain value. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding." -->

**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet, individual participant data; 6 primary prevention trials, ~95,000 people)**
- Benefit: 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions (0.18% vs 0.23% per year); net effect on stroke not significant, vascular mortality unchanged (0.19% vs 0.19%). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials, 164,225 participants, median baseline cardiovascular risk 9.2%)**
- Benefit: composite cardiovascular outcome 57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89 (95% credible interval 0.84–0.95); absolute risk reduction 0.38%; number needed to treat 265. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"(hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)"} -->

- Framing: not a verdict but a trade-off to discuss — lower cardiovascular risk alongside increased major bleeding, information that "may inform discussions with patients." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

answer:
**Populations enrolled**

- **ARRIVE:** men aged ≥55 years and women aged ≥60 years with average risk deemed moderate by number of risk factors; patients at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes were excluded. 12,546 patients were randomized at 501 sites (aspirin 6,270 vs placebo 6,276), median follow-up 60 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->
- **ASPREE:** community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged ≥70 years, or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US, without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability; 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin vs placebo, enrollment 2010–2014. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
- **JPPP:** 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60–85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus, recruited at 1,007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years; open-label 100 mg/day aspirin vs no aspirin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations (population: adults ≥40 without CVD and not at increased bleeding risk)** <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD"} -->

- **Aged 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** individual decision; small net benefit (C recommendation), and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Aged ≥60:** recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation); moderate certainty of no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

**Relation to the trial evidence:** The three trials enrolled almost entirely people aged 60 and older (JPPP 60–85; ARRIVE men ≥55/women ≥60; ASPREE ≥70, or ≥65 in US black and Hispanic participants), so they bear on the ≥60 recommendation rather than the 40–59 group. Their results are consistent with the D recommendation: in ASPREE, low-dose aspirin did not significantly lower cardiovascular disease but significantly increased major hemorrhage, <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo"} --> with higher all-cause mortality attributed mainly to cancer-related death, <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death."} --> and in JPPP the 5-year primary outcome rate did not differ significantly (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77–1.15). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} --> ARRIVE found no significant reduction in its primary composite endpoint (4.29% vs 4.48%; HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)"} -->

The knowledge base does not state explicitly which trials the USPSTF used to support each recommendation, nor does it contain trial evidence for the 40–59 age group.

**ARRIVE** — men aged 55 years and older and women aged 60 years and older with average cardiovascular risk, judged moderate by number of risk factors; patients at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes were excluded. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->

**ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 or older (or ≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->

**JPPP** — 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus, recruited at 1007 primary care clinics in Japan. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan"} -->

**USPSTF (2022)** — for adults 40 to 59 years with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk, moderate certainty of a small net benefit; the decision to start low-dose aspirin should be individual (C recommendation), especially for those not at increased bleeding risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> For adults 60 or older, moderate certainty of no net benefit, and the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older."} -->

Relation to the trials: all three trials enrolled populations aged 60 or older (ARRIVE women and JPPP from 60; ASPREE from 65/70), i.e., within the age band for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation; none of them tested the 40–59-year group that the C recommendation addresses. The knowledge base's documents do not otherwise state how the USPSTF graded or weighed these specific trials.

In JPPP, the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was 2.77% (95% CI, 2.40%–3.20%) with aspirin versus 2.96% (95% CI, 2.58%–3.40%) without aspirin — not significantly different (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77–1.15; P = .54), in patients aged 60–85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes (N = 14,464). Source: "Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in Japanese patients 60 years or older with atherosclerotic risk factors: a randomized clinical trial."

answer:
**ASPREE** (healthy adults ≥70 years, or ≥65 for US blacks/Hispanics; 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin vs placebo; 19,114 participants, median 4.7 years): all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.29), with 1052 deaths <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)."} -->. Cancer was the major contributor, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years; cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% vs 2.3% (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56) <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56)."} -->. The authors called this unexpected and to be interpreted with caution <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution."} -->.

**ASCEND** (adults with diabetes, no evident cardiovascular disease; aspirin 100 mg daily): there was no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 [2.0%] vs 158 [2.0%]) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] vs 887 [11.5%]), with long-term follow-up planned <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned."} -->. Its conclusion was that aspirin prevented serious vascular events but caused major bleeding, with absolute benefits largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events."} -->.

**ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients without diabetes, 12,546 randomised, median 60 months): the primary composite endpoint occurred in 4.29% with aspirin vs 4.48% with placebo (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038) <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)."} -->.

**Comparison:** ASPREE is the only one of the three reporting a statistically significant excess in all-cause mortality, driven by cancer deaths; ASCEND found no significant difference in cancer incidence, and the knowledge base does not give ARRIVE's all-cause mortality or cancer results, nor ASCEND's all-cause mortality figures, so those comparisons cannot be made from it.

answer:
**ASPREE** (100 mg enteric-coated aspirin vs placebo; 19,114 adults ≥70 years, or ≥65 for US Black/Hispanic participants, free of CVD, dementia and disability): all-cause mortality was 12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.29), with cancer the major contributor, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years; cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% vs 2.3% (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56). The authors call this unexpected and to be interpreted with caution. *Effect of Aspirin on All-Cause Mortality in the Healthy Elderly*
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution."} -->

**ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients without diabetes, median follow-up 60 months): no mortality signal — 321 documented deaths, 160 (2.55%) with aspirin vs 161 (2.57%) with placebo; the only significant excess was gastrointestinal bleeding (0.97% vs 0.46%; HR 2.11). No cancer findings are reported in the retrieved text. *Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events in patients at moderate risk of cardiovascular disease (ARRIVE)*
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)."} -->

**ASCEND** (diabetes without evident CVD, mean follow-up 7.4 years): serious vascular events were reduced (8.5% vs 9.6%; rate ratio 0.88) at the cost of major bleeding (4.1% vs 3.2%; rate ratio 1.29); there was no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer (2.0% vs 2.0%) or all cancers (11.6% vs 11.5%), with long-term follow-up planned. All-cause mortality figures are not given in the retrieved text. *Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus*
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%])"} -->

So ASPREE's excess all-cause and cancer mortality is not replicated in ARRIVE (equal deaths) or ASCEND (no cancer incidence difference); ASCEND's trade-off is vascular benefit against bleeding.

JPPP was terminated early by the data monitoring committee on the basis of likely futility, after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55–5.33). The trial was an open-label comparison of enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d versus no aspirin in 14,464 patients aged 60–85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes; the 5-year cumulative primary outcome rate did not differ significantly (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77–1.15; P = .54).

Source: "Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in Japanese patients 60 years or older with atherosclerotic risk factors: a randomized clinical trial."
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility."} -->

answer:
In ASCEND (Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus):

- **Randomized: 15,480 participants** — adults with diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization."} -->
- **Aspirin dose: 100 mg daily** (or matching placebo), given to adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at entry. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo." -->

**Populations enrolled**

- **ARRIVE**: men aged ≥55 years and women aged ≥60 years with average, "moderate" cardiovascular risk based on risk-factor count; patients at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes were excluded. 12,546 patients enrolled at 501 sites in seven countries. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->
- **ASPREE**: community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the US aged ≥70 years (≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability; 19,114 enrolled. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
- **JPPP**: Japanese patients aged 60–85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics; N = 14,464. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations (2022 statement) and how they relate**

- Population addressed: adults ≥40 years without signs/symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased bleeding risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->
- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk**: moderate certainty of a *small net benefit*; decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual (C recommendation). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older**: moderate certainty of *no net benefit*; recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older."} -->

**Relation to the trial evidence**: all three trials enrolled populations at or above the age-60 threshold of the D recommendation (ARRIVE women ≥60, JPPP 60–85, ASPREE ≥70/≥65), and none showed a significant reduction in cardiovascular events — ASPREE found no significant CVD reduction with more major hemorrhage, and JPPP was stopped for futility. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility."} --> ARRIVE's narrower age entry for men (≥55) is the only trial population overlapping the 40–59 band, and it too showed no significant benefit (HR 0.96) with doubled GI bleeding. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)"} --> The knowledge base does not state explicitly how the USPSTF weighed these individual trials.

In ASCEND (Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus):

- **Randomized: 15,480 participants** — adults with diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization."} -->
- **Aspirin dose: 100 mg daily** (or matching placebo), given to adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at entry. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo." -->

In JPPP (Japanese Primary Prevention Project, N = 14,464 patients aged 60–85 with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes; aspirin 100 mg/d vs no aspirin), the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between groups: **2.77% (95% CI, 2.40%–3.20%) with aspirin vs 2.96% (95% CI, 2.58%–3.40%) without aspirin; HR 0.94 (95% CI, 0.77–1.15); P = .54**.

Source: "Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in Japanese patients 60 years or older with atherosclerotic risk factors: a randomized clinical trial" (JAMA 2014).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} -->
