answer: In ASCEND (Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus), 15,480 participants underwent randomization. They received aspirin 100 mg daily or matching placebo, in adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo." -->

**ARRIVE** enrolled men aged 55 or older and women aged 60 or older with average (moderate) cardiovascular risk based on risk-factor count, excluding those at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes; 12,546 patients were randomized (aspirin 100 mg vs placebo) at 501 sites in seven countries (Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events in patients at moderate risk of cardiovascular disease (ARRIVE)).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

**ASPREE** enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the US aged 70 or older (or ≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability; 19,114 participants, median follow-up 4.7 years (Effect of Aspirin on Cardiovascular Events and Bleeding in the Healthy Elderly).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"Of the 19,114 persons who were enrolled in the trial, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo."} -->

**JPPP** enrolled 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus, recruited at 1007 clinics in Japan (open-label, low-dose aspirin vs no aspirin) (Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in Japanese patients 60 years or older with atherosclerotic risk factors).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan"} -->

**USPSTF (2022)** covers adults 40 or older without CVD and not at increased bleeding risk; it concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin for primary prevention in adults aged 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit (individual decision, C recommendation), and with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin in adults 60 or older has no net benefit (recommends against, D recommendation) (Aspirin Use to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} -->

Relation to the evidence: the trials bear directly on the ≥60 age band. ASPREE found no significant reduction in CVD with aspirin in healthy older adults but a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage (8.6 vs 6.2 events per 1000 person-years; HR 1.38), and higher all-cause mortality attributed mainly to cancer deaths (Effect of Aspirin on Cardiovascular Events and Bleeding in the Healthy Elderly; Effect of Aspirin on All-Cause Mortality in the Healthy Elderly). JPPP's population (60–85 years with risk factors) likewise sits entirely in the ≥60 group. ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60) straddles the boundary, so it speaks only partly to the 40–59 band — none of the three trials enrolled a substantial population aged 40–59, so the small-net-benefit judgment for that age group rests on evidence outside these three trials (the USPSTF statement describes a commissioned systematic review and modeling study but does not itself list which trials enrolled which ages).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death."} -->

In JPPP (Japanese Primary Prevention Project; N = 14,464, patients aged 60–85 with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes, median follow-up 5.02 years, stopped early for futility):

- 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate with aspirin: 2.77% (95% CI, 2.40%–3.20%)
- 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate without aspirin: 2.96% (95% CI, 2.58%–3.40%)
- Hazard ratio: 0.94 (95% CI, 0.77–1.15); P = .54 — i.e., not significantly different between groups.

All from the JPPP randomized trial report.

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} -->

Both documents are short and fully read.

**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet, individual-participant data, 6 primary prevention trials, ~95,000 people)** — benefit: a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions (0.18% vs 0.23% per year); no significant effect on stroke or vascular mortality. Harm: increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), with coronary risk factors also predicting bleeding. Net balance: framed as *uncertain* — "aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)"} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials, 164,225 participants)** — benefit: composite of cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke reduced, HR 0.89 (95% CrI 0.84–0.95), absolute risk reduction 0.38% (0.20%–0.55%), NNT 265 (57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years). Harm: major bleeding increased, HR 1.43 (1.30–1.56), absolute risk increase 0.47% (0.34%–0.62%), NNH 210 (23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years). Net balance: framed as a trade-off to inform shared decision-making, without a verdict for or against — "This information may inform discussions with patients about aspirin for primary prevention." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"This information may inform discussions with patients about aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events and bleeding."} -->

**Comparison:** the 2009 analysis reports only relative/proportional effects and per-year event rates, so it gives no absolute benefit-versus-harm arithmetic; the 2019 analysis puts both on the same absolute scale and shows the absolute bleeding increase (0.47%) slightly exceeding the absolute cardiovascular reduction (0.38%), with NNH 210 vs NNT 265 — i.e., in that population the net absolute balance is unfavourable, whereas 2009 called the net value "uncertain." Neither document quantifies a combined net clinical benefit outcome.

**ARRIVE** (Lancet, 2018): men aged 55+ and women aged 60+, at average/moderate cardiovascular risk based on number of risk factors, in seven countries; patients at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes were excluded. 12,546 patients were randomised (aspirin 6270, placebo 6276) at 501 sites, median follow-up 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% vs 4.48% (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->

answer: In ASCEND (Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus), 15,480 participants underwent randomization. They received aspirin 100 mg daily or matching placebo, in adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo." -->

**2009 Lancet collaborative meta-analysis** (individual participant data; 6 primary prevention trials, ~95,000 people): aspirin produced a **12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events** (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions; the net effect on stroke was not significant, and vascular mortality did not differ (0.19% vs 0.19% per year). Bleeding harm: **major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds increased** (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001). Framing: **net value "uncertain"** — the reduction in occlusive events must be weighed against the increase in major bleeds.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds"} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis** (13 trials, 164,225 participants): aspirin was associated with a **lower composite cardiovascular outcome** — 57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years (HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84–0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%, NNT 265) — and with **increased major bleeding** — 23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years (HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30–1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%, NNH 210). Framing: the conclusion is **descriptive rather than adjudicative** — lower cardiovascular risk with higher bleeding risk, information to inform patient discussions rather than a verdict of net benefit or harm.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"(hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"(HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

**Comparison:** the relative cardiovascular benefit is of similar magnitude (12% proportional reduction vs HR 0.89), but the absolute terms differ in scale and the bleeding harm is framed more sharply in 2019 (HR 1.43, absolute increase 0.47%) than in 2009 (0.10% vs 0.07% per year), where the harm was reported as a per-year rate difference. On net balance, 2009 explicitly called net value "uncertain" pending further trials, whereas 2019 avoided a net-value judgment and presented the two effects side by side for shared decision-making. The knowledge base does not give a direct head-to-head statistical comparison of the two analyses' effect estimates.

answer:
**ASPREE** (19,114 adults ≥70, or ≥65 for US blacks/Hispanics, free of CVD/dementia/disability; 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin vs placebo; median 4.7 years): all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.29), with 1052 deaths. Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% vs 2.3% (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56), cancer being the major contributor, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years; the authors called this unexpected and to be interpreted with caution.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years."} -->

**ARRIVE** (12,546 moderate-CVD-risk patients, 100 mg aspirin vs placebo, median 60 months): no mortality excess — 321 deaths, 160 (2.55%) with aspirin vs 161 (2.57%) with placebo. The knowledge base does not report cancer outcomes for ARRIVE.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)."} -->

**ASCEND** (diabetes without evident CVD, 100 mg aspirin vs placebo): no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 [2.0%] vs 158 [2.0%]) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] vs 887 [11.5%]), with long-term follow-up planned. The knowledge base does not give ASCEND's all-cause mortality figures.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%])"} -->

So ASPREE's excess mortality and cancer deaths stand alone among these three: ARRIVE showed essentially identical death rates in both arms, and ASCEND showed no cancer incidence difference. Note the populations differ (older adults vs moderate-risk vs diabetes), and ASPREE's own authors caution against over-interpretation.

**Trial populations**

- **ARRIVE** (Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events…): men aged 55 and older and women aged 60 and older with average, i.e. moderate, cardiovascular risk based on the number of specific risk factors; patients at high bleeding risk and those with diabetes were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
- **ASPREE** (Effect of Aspirin on Cardiovascular Events and Bleeding in the Healthy Elderly): community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 or older (≥65 among Blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability; 19,114 enrolled. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
- **JPPP** (Low-dose aspirin for primary prevention… Japanese patients): 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes, recruited at 1007 clinics in Japan. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations** (Aspirin Use to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease, 2022)

- Adults 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk: moderate certainty of a small net benefit; the decision to start low-dose aspirin should be individual (C recommendation). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
- Adults 60 or older: moderate certainty of no net benefit; the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)." -->

**Relation to the evidence:** the recommendation statement's scope is adults 40 or older without CVD who are not at increased bleeding risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} --> All three trials enrolled populations that sit in the ≥60-year-old group for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation: ARRIVE's participants were all ≥55 (men) / ≥60 (women), ASPREE's all ≥65–70, and JPPP's all 60–85 — so none of the three directly informs the 40–59 recommendation. The recommendation document itself does not name ARRIVE, ASPREE or JPPP in the sections available here, so the specific weight given to each trial is not stated in the knowledge base.

JPPP (the Japanese Primary Prevention Project) was terminated early by its data monitoring committee on the basis of likely futility, after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55–5.33). The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between groups (2.77% with aspirin vs 2.96% without; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77–1.15; P = .54).

The 2019 JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (Zheng et al.) included **13 trials randomizing 164,225 participants**, with 1,050,511 participant-years of follow-up; this applies to trials enrolling ≥1000 participants without known cardiovascular disease and ≥12 months of follow-up.
